weekly-01.subject: What stopped you last time
weekly-01.preview: An excuse explains one bad week. A pattern explains all of them.
weekly-01.html:
An excuse explains one bad week. A pattern explains all of them.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · STEP 3

Pattern, not excuse.

You’ve set goals like the ones on last week’s list before. Some of them more than once. Before you build anything new, look honestly at why the last attempt didn’t hold.

An excuse explains one bad week: work was crazy, the kids were sick. A pattern explains why it happens every time.

An example. A man tries three times to start praying in the morning. Every attempt dies the first week he stays up past midnight. The obstacle was never prayer. It was that his evenings had no end time. That is something a system can fix.

Four questions to push past your first answer:

  • When exactly did the last attempt stop, and what was happening that day?

  • Did the goal ever have a set time, or only good intentions?

  • Who knew about it, and did anyone notice when it stopped?

  • What did you tell yourself the first time you missed?

Be specific and be fair. Guilt is a mood, and moods don’t build anything. You’re making a list of what your system has to survive.

THE TIME

Fifteen minutes, one evening this week. Pick it now.

THE TRIGGER

The goal you’ve restarted the most times. Start with that one.

THE TEST

You’ve written down one obstacle you’ve never said out loud.

If you’re willing, hit reply and name the pattern you found. Saying it to another man is half of fixing it. Inside the Club, the monthly call and your accountability partner are where men do exactly that.

weekly-02.subject: “This week” is not a time
weekly-02.preview: Four rules for a promise that survives an ordinary week.
weekly-02.html:
Four rules for a promise that survives an ordinary week.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · STEP 4

“This week” is not a time.

You have a sentence, a short list of goals, and an honest look at what stopped you. Now they have to live somewhere other than your head.

A goal says what. A system says when. These four rules turn one into the other. They’re the rules behind the Weekly Scorecard:

  1. Write the when. Every decision gets a time and a place before the week starts. “Tuesday and Thursday, 9 pm, after the kids are down” is a time. “This week” is not.

  2. Define the miss. Decide in advance what counts as a miss, so a bad week is defined before, not argued about after.

  3. Log it that day. Sunday-night memory is a story, not evidence.

  4. Run the wife test. Could the people in your house see it without you announcing it? If not, it didn’t hold.

Go back to the man whose morning prayer kept dying on late nights. His system doesn’t just say “pray at 6 am.” It says when his evening ends, what counts as a miss, and what he does the morning after one.

Missing once is not failure. The sheet tells you exactly what is.

THE TIME

Sunday, fifteen minutes, before the week starts.

THE TRIGGER

Your three goals from Step 2, and the obstacle from Step 3.

THE TEST

Every goal has a when, a miss and a wife test written next to it.

weekly-03.subject: The empty pillar
weekly-03.preview: Most men’s goals pile up in one or two places and leave one empty.
weekly-03.html:
Most men’s goals pile up in one or two places and leave one empty.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · STEP 5

The empty pillar.

A man can hold one area of his life together for a while by letting the others slide. He gets serious at work and disappears at home. He fixes his health and stops praying. From the inside it feels like progress. From the kitchen table it looks like a trade.

Step 5 exists to stop that trade. The framework rests on four pillars. Each one carries weight, and the whole thing leans when one is ignored.

You can run the check this week, even before you have the worksheet:

  1. List the areas of your life where other people depend on you. For most men that is some version of their faith, their marriage, their kids, and their work.

  2. Take the goals you scheduled with last week’s four rules and put each one under the area it serves.

  3. Circle the area with nothing under it.

Most men find the same thing. Their goals pile up under one or two areas, and one sits empty.

An empty pillar is not a failure. It’s information. It’s often exactly where the obstacle you found in Step 3 was hiding, because nothing in your plan was protecting it.

THE TIME

Your Sunday planning, ten extra minutes.

THE TRIGGER

Your scheduled goals, sorted by the area of life each one serves.

THE TEST

The empty area now has one small decision with a time on it.

weekly-04.subject: A mechanism, not a mood
weekly-04.preview: Two men, the same goal, three months later.
weekly-04.html:
Two men, the same goal, three months later.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · STEP 6

A mechanism, not a mood.

Picture two men with the same goal: a weekly date night with their wives.

The first man plans to do it “when things calm down.” The second has Friday at 7 written down, a sitter booked on the first of every month, and a rule that a cancelled Friday moves to Saturday, never to “sometime.”

Three months later, only one of them is still going on dates. Both of them meant it.

The difference isn’t character. One built a mechanism. The other relied on a mood. That’s Step 6: why you need a system.

If you’ve followed along these five weeks, you already have the parts:

  1. The sentence that says who you’re becoming

  2. Three goals that pass it

  3. The pattern that stopped you before

  4. A when, a miss and a wife test for each goal

  5. No empty pillar

This week, put it all on one page. Put your Sunday review in your calendar as a repeating event. And decide who you’ll tell when you miss: your wife, a friend, or other men doing the same work.

THE TIME

A weekly Sunday review, same time every week, on the calendar.

THE TRIGGER

The calendar alert. Not your mood.

THE TEST

Your system fits on one page and runs on a week you don’t feel like it.

There’s one step left. Step 7 is God at the center. A system built only on your own strength eventually runs into the limits of your own strength. The goal was never to become a more efficient version of yourself. It was to become the man God is calling you to be, and to let the system serve that.

weekly-05.subject: The first ten minutes home
weekly-05.preview: The most important part of your evening happens at the door.
weekly-05.html:
The most important part of your evening happens at the door.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · MECHANISM 1

The first ten minutes home.

The framework is finished. From here, every Thursday is one mechanism: a single decision with a time, a trigger and a test, built for an ordinary week.

We start at the door.

Most men come home still at work. The phone is in the hand, the last meeting is still in the head, and the first thing the family gets is a man who is physically there and mentally in the car. Nobody decided that. It just happens, every night, because nothing was built to stop it.

The first ten minutes set the tone for the whole evening. So give them a shape:

  1. Finish work in the driveway. Two minutes in the car. Send the last message, then put the phone face down.

  2. Phone in the drawer by the door. Not in your pocket. In the drawer.

  3. Find your wife first. One real question, not “how was your day.” Try “what was the hardest part of today?”

  4. Then each kid. Get down to their level for one minute each.

THE TIME

Every weeknight, the first ten minutes after you park.

THE TRIGGER

The engine turns off. That’s the cue, not your mood.

THE TEST

By Friday, would your wife say evenings felt different? Ask her.

Put it on your Weekly Scorecard as one of this week’s decisions, with the miss defined: phone out of the drawer before the kids are in bed.

weekly-06.subject: Fifteen minutes on Sunday
weekly-06.preview: The review that decides whether the week holds, step by step.
weekly-06.html:
The review that decides whether the week holds, step by step.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · MECHANISM 2

Fifteen minutes on Sunday.

Every system breaks eventually. What separates the men whose systems last from the men who start over every January is not that their weeks go well. It’s that they look at the week honestly before the next one starts.

That’s the Sunday review. Fifteen minutes. Here is exactly how to run it:

  1. Read your sentence. The one from Step 1. Out loud if you can. Everything else gets measured against it.

  2. Score the week from the page, not from memory. Which decisions held? Which didn’t? If you didn’t log it on the day, count it as unknown, not as a win.

  3. Name the trigger for every miss. A time that was never realistic? A situation you didn’t plan for? Or no decision at all?

  4. Change one thing. One. Move a time, shrink a decision, or add a backup plan for the trigger that got you.

  5. Pray over the week ahead. Specifically. The Tuesday you already know will be hard.

Missing once is not failure. A miss you never name is.

THE TIME

Sunday, same time every week. Put it in your calendar now as a repeating event.

THE TRIGGER

The calendar alert. Coffee, your scorecard, and a pen.

THE TEST

You finish with one written change for next week. Not a feeling. A change.

weekly-07.subject: Say it at the table
weekly-07.preview: “I’m thankful for my family” doesn’t count. Here’s what does.
weekly-07.html:
“I’m thankful for my family” doesn’t count. Here’s what does.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · THANKSGIVING

Say it at the table.

Happy Thanksgiving. This one is short, because today should be spent with them, not with your inbox.

Somewhere today, someone will go around the table and ask what everyone is thankful for. Most men will say “my family.” It’s true. It’s also the kind of thing nobody at the table will remember by Friday.

Gratitude that is specific gets remembered. So before dinner, take five minutes and write one sentence for your wife and one for each child. Not what they are. Something they did.

Here is the difference. “I’m thankful for your mom” versus “I’m thankful your mom sat up with your brother three nights in a row when he was sick, and never once complained.” One is a greeting card. The other is a moment a kid will repeat years from now.

Then say them out loud at the table. Say your wife’s first.

THE TIME

Five minutes before the meal. Write them down.

THE TRIGGER

Someone asks “what are you thankful for?” Or you ask it first.

THE TEST

Could each of them repeat back what you said about them tomorrow?

weekly-08.subject: The conversation you keep postponing
weekly-08.preview: “When things calm down” is not a date. Put it on the calendar.
weekly-08.html:
“When things calm down” is not a date. Put it on the calendar.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · MECHANISM 3

The conversation you keep postponing.

Every man has one. Money with your wife. An apology you owe. The talk with your son about what he’s looking at on his phone. You know exactly which one it is for you.

You’ve been waiting for the right moment. Here is the problem: the right moment is a mood, and moods don’t schedule themselves. The conversation keeps getting pushed to “when things calm down,” and things never calm down.

So treat it like anything else in your system. Give it a when.

  1. Name it in one sentence. Write down what the conversation is actually about. If you can’t say it in one sentence, you’re not ready to have it.

  2. Pick a time and ask for it. “Can we talk Saturday morning after breakfast? There’s something I’ve been putting off.” Asking ahead takes the ambush out of it.

  3. Write your first line. The hardest part is starting. Try: “I’ve been avoiding this, and that’s on me.”

  4. Listen more than you talk. Your job in the first ten minutes is to understand, not to win.

THE TIME

A specific day and hour within the next seven days.

THE TRIGGER

You ask for the time today. Out loud, not in your head.

THE TEST

By next Thursday, the conversation has happened. Not gone well. Happened.

weekly-09.subject: The best meeting of your day
weekly-09.preview: Ten minutes at bedtime. Three questions. No phone.
weekly-09.html:
Ten minutes at bedtime. Three questions. No phone.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · MECHANISM 4

The best meeting of your day.

At the dinner table, kids give one-word answers. “Good.” “Fine.” “Nothing.” Then the lights go off, and suddenly they want to talk about everything. Anyone who has put a child to bed knows this.

That isn’t a stalling tactic. It’s the one time of day when the house is quiet, the screens are off, and they have your full attention in the dark. It’s the best meeting of your day, and most fathers skip it because they’re tired and bedtime has become something to get through.

Turn it into a mechanism. Ten minutes, sitting on the edge of the bed, with three questions:

  1. “What was the best part of today?” Easy to answer. It gets them talking.

  2. “Was anything hard today?” Then wait. The pause is where the real answer comes.

  3. “What can I pray for?” Then pray for it, right there, out loud and short.

Kids too old for tuck-ins? Same questions, in the car, on the drive to practice. Side by side works better than face to face for most teenagers anyway.

THE TIME

Three nights this week. Pick them now.

THE TRIGGER

The light switch. Phone stays in the drawer from the first ten minutes home.

THE TEST

You know one thing about their week you wouldn’t have known otherwise.

weekly-10.subject: The smallest version that still counts
weekly-10.preview: December is coming for your system. Shrink it before it breaks.
weekly-10.html:
December is coming for your system. Shrink it before it breaks.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · MECHANISM 5

The smallest version that still counts.

The next two weeks will break more systems than any other part of the year. Travel, family in the house, kids off school, late nights, a different schedule every day. The plan that worked in October won’t survive it.

Most men respond by pausing everything until January. “I’ll start again after the holidays.” Then January comes, and they’re starting from zero, again.

Don’t pause the system. Shrink it. Build a holiday version that is so small it survives anything:

  1. Keep one decision per pillar. Cut everything else until January. One for faith, one for your marriage, one for your kids.

  2. Shrink each one until it fits a bad day. Not thirty minutes of prayer. Five. Not date night. Ten minutes on the porch after the house goes quiet.

  3. Attach it to something that will still happen. Your routine is gone, but coffee, meals and bedtime aren’t. Hook each decision to one of those.

  4. Keep the Sunday review. Even five minutes of it. That’s what makes January a continuation, not a restart.

THE TIME

This Sunday: write your holiday version before the week starts.

THE TRIGGER

Coffee, meals and bedtime. The things December can’t cancel.

THE TEST

On January 2nd you’re continuing, not starting over.

weekly-11.subject: One evening before January
weekly-11.preview: A year-end review that ends with a plan, not a resolution.
weekly-11.html:
A year-end review that ends with a plan, not a resolution.

THE THURSDAY EMAIL · MECHANISM 6

One evening before January.

Merry Christmas. Enjoy today and tomorrow. This one is for later in the week.

In a week, most men will make New Year’s resolutions. You already know how that goes: you’ll mean it, and by February it will be gone. A resolution is a feeling on a date. A plan has a when.

So instead, pick one evening between Christmas and New Year’s and give it an hour. Five questions, on paper:

  1. Read your sentence. Is it still true? Change it if it isn’t.

  2. Name three things that held this year, with evidence. Not “I was a better dad.” What actually happened, and when.

  3. Name the one pattern that cost you the most. The trigger that kept winning. Be specific.

  4. Pick one decision per pillar for January. Each with a time, a miss and a test. Three or four decisions, not twelve.

  5. Read it to your wife. Ask her what she’d add. She’s seen your year from the other side of the table.

THE TIME

One evening between Dec 26 and Dec 31. Pick it today.

THE TRIGGER

The house goes quiet. An hour, a pen, the five questions.

THE TEST

January 1st, you have a written plan. Not a resolution.

welcome-2.subject: Did you write the sentence?
welcome-2.preview: Twenty minutes, a pen, and the one question most men skip.
welcome-2.html:
Twenty minutes, a pen, and the one question most men skip.

BE THE MAN · STEP 1

Did you write the sentence?

Most men who download Step 1 still have it sitting in a downloads folder a month later. Not because they didn’t mean it. Because “I’ll do it this weekend” is not a time.

So this week, one thing: finish Step 1. One question: what type of man do you want to be? Not in the abstract. On an ordinary Tuesday.

Work it in four moves:

  1. Name the attributes. Patient. Present. Faithful. Your words, not ones that sound good.

  2. Make each one ordinary. “Patient” becomes “I don’t raise my voice when homework runs late.”

  3. Apply the house test. How would the people you live with know, without being told?

  4. Write the sentence that says who he is.

Here is the kind of sentence you’re aiming for: “I am a man who is home when he is home, keeps his word to his wife, and lets his kids see him pray.” Every part can be checked on a given day. Every part is visible to someone else.

THE TIME

Tonight or Friday night. Twenty minutes, one sitting.

THE TRIGGER

The house goes down. Pen and paper, phone in another room.

THE TEST

Could someone in your house notice each part of your sentence without being told?

Print it. It was built for paper, not for a screen you’ll close. When you’ve written the sentence, put it where you’ll see it every Sunday.

welcome-3.subject: Fewer goals than you think
welcome-3.preview: Your sentence is the filter. Most goals won’t pass it.
welcome-3.html:
Your sentence is the filter. Most goals won’t pass it.

BE THE MAN · STEP 2

Fewer goals than you think.

The last email was the sentence. This one makes it earn its keep.

A goal set before Step 1 is chosen by mood: whatever felt urgent that week. A goal set after it is chosen because the man in your sentence would pursue it.

So put your sentence in front of you and ask one question of every goal: does this move me toward that man, or is it just something I feel I should want?

An example. If your sentence says “home when he is home,” then “phone off from 6 to 8 on weeknights” passes. “Read fifty books this year” might be a fine goal, but unless it serves the sentence, it doesn’t go on this list yet.

Four mistakes men make at this step:

  • Ten goals when three would actually get done

  • Goals so vague you could never tell if you missed one

  • Borrowed goals that didn’t come from your sentence

  • A goal with no idea when in the week it happens

That last one gets fixed later in the framework. For now, get the right goals on paper, and fewer of them than you think.

THE TIME

Sunday evening. Fifteen minutes.

THE TRIGGER

Your Step 1 sentence on the table before you write a single goal.

THE TEST

Three goals or fewer, and you can name the part of the sentence each one serves.

BE THE MAN · STEP 4

“This week” is not a time.

You have a sentence, a short list of goals, and an honest look at what stopped you. Now they have to live somewhere other than your head.

A goal says what. A system says when. These four rules turn one into the other. They’re the rules behind the Weekly Scorecard:

  1. Write the when. Every decision gets a time and a place before the week starts. “Tuesday and Thursday, 9 pm, after the kids are down” is a time. “This week” is not.

  2. Define the miss. Decide in advance what counts as a miss, so a bad week is defined before, not argued about after.

  3. Log it that day. Sunday-night memory is a story, not evidence.

  4. Run the wife test. Could the people in your house see it without you announcing it? If not, it didn’t hold.

Go back to the man whose morning prayer kept dying on late nights. His system doesn’t just say “pray at 6 am.” It says when his evening ends, what counts as a miss, and what he does the morning after one.

Missing once is not failure. The sheet tells you exactly what is.

THE TIME

Sunday, fifteen minutes, before the week starts.

THE TRIGGER

Your three goals from Step 2, and the obstacle from Step 3.

THE TEST

Every goal has a when, a miss and a wife test written next to it.

welcome-6.preview: Most men’s goals pile up in one or two places and leave one empty.
welcome-6.html:
Most men’s goals pile up in one or two places and leave one empty.

BE THE MAN · STEP 5

The empty pillar.

A man can hold one area of his life together for a while by letting the others slide. He gets serious at work and disappears at home. He fixes his health and stops praying. From the inside it feels like progress. From the kitchen table it looks like a trade.

Step 5 exists to stop that trade. The framework rests on four pillars. Each one carries weight, and the whole thing leans when one is ignored.

You can run the check this week, even before you have the worksheet:

  1. List the areas of your life where other people depend on you. For most men that is some version of their faith, their marriage, their kids, and their work.

  2. Take the goals you scheduled with the four rules from the last email and put each one under the area it serves.

  3. Circle the area with nothing under it.

Most men find the same thing. Their goals pile up under one or two areas, and one sits empty.

An empty pillar is not a failure. It’s information. It’s often exactly where the obstacle you found in Step 3 was hiding, because nothing in your plan was protecting it.

THE TIME

Your Sunday planning, ten extra minutes.

THE TRIGGER

Your scheduled goals, sorted by the area of life each one serves.

THE TEST

The empty area now has one small decision with a time on it.

welcome-7.subject: A mechanism, not a mood
welcome-7.preview: Two men, the same goal, three months later.
welcome-7.html:
Two men, the same goal, three months later.

BE THE MAN · STEP 6

A mechanism, not a mood.

Picture two men with the same goal: a weekly date night with their wives.

The first man plans to do it “when things calm down.” The second has Friday at 7 written down, a sitter booked on the first of every month, and a rule that a cancelled Friday moves to Saturday, never to “sometime.”

Three months later, only one of them is still going on dates. Both of them meant it.

The difference isn’t character. One built a mechanism. The other relied on a mood. That’s Step 6: why you need a system.

If you’ve followed along with these emails, you already have the parts:

  1. The sentence that says who you’re becoming

  2. Three goals that pass it

  3. The pattern that stopped you before

  4. A when, a miss and a wife test for each goal

  5. No empty pillar

This week, put it all on one page. Put your Sunday review in your calendar as a repeating event. And decide who you’ll tell when you miss: your wife, a friend, or other men doing the same work.

THE TIME

A weekly Sunday review, same time every week, on the calendar.

THE TRIGGER

The calendar alert. Not your mood.

THE TEST

Your system fits on one page and runs on a week you don’t feel like it.

There’s one step left. Step 7 is God at the center. A system built only on your own strength eventually runs into the limits of your own strength. The goal was never to become a more efficient version of yourself. It was to become the man God is calling you to be, and to let the system serve that.
